title: Mark Fisher
summary: Mark Fisher was a British philosopher, music critic and teacher who wrote about how the economy and culture seep into the way we feel. His “capitalist realism” is the widespread sense that the existing order is the only one possible and that an alternative to it can’t even be imagined. Fisher combined analysis of pop music, film and everyday life with one question: why do so many people feel exhausted and depressed?
onEmotions: Fisher’s central idea about feelings is that they can’t be fully understood if we look only inside a single person. He called this “the privatization of stress”: society teaches us to regard anxiety, depression and fatigue as purely personal problems, although they also have social causes — precarious work, competition, debt, a sense that the future has been closed off. This view doesn’t cancel your personal history, but it lifts some of the guilt. Fisher also wrote about “hauntology” — the feeling of being haunted by the ghosts of futures that never arrived — and about how collectively recognizing shared difficulties can itself bring relief.

anxiety.text: If millions of people are anxious, can that really be a million separate malfunctions? Fisher began his conversation about mental health with this question, and your anxiety deserves compassion, not reproach. He wrote about “the privatization of stress”: we are taught to see anxiety as a strictly personal malfunction — faulty brain chemistry or a weak character — even though many of its sources lie outside us. Unstable work, constant evaluation, the need to keep “selling yourself,” an unclear tomorrow — all this creates a background against which anxiety is natural. Knowing this can lighten the load. Your anxiety is not only your fault; it is also a response to real conditions that many people share with you.
anxiety.practice: Say one sentence to someone you trust: “What’s worrying me right now is…” — and then ask: “And you?” Fisher saw such conversations as the first step toward anxiety no longer being private.

quote.text: The current ruling ontology denies any possibility of a social causation of mental illness.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

fear.text: The word “flexibility” sounds like freedom, but Fisher advised listening to it more closely. Your fear is a natural reaction to uncertainty, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Fisher described a world in which uncertainty has become the norm: a job can end at any moment, the future isn’t guaranteed, and responsibility for everything is placed on the individual. He noted that the flexibility and instability presented as freedom turn, for many people, into chronic fear. Taking Fisher’s thought further, fear is not only a personal trait but a reasonable response to conditions in which a person has little to lean on. This understanding helps you stop blaming yourself for being afraid. And it suggests where to look for support: not only in your own resilience, but in other people who fear the same things.
fear.practice: Stand up, press your feet into the floor and feel that the floor holds not only you but everyone in this building. Take three slow out-breaths with the thought that support can be shared.

sadness.text: Fisher noted that depression had become one of the most common conditions in Britain — and yet it is still treated as a strictly private misfortune. Sadness doesn’t need to be hidden behind a cheerful smile. He noticed that in a culture demanding constant positivity and “motivation,” sadness looks like personal failure. But in his view, sorrow often responds to a real loss — the loss of community, of stability, of faith in a better future. Fisher wrote about “the slow cancellation of the future”: the feeling that the new things progress promised never actually arrived. In this light, your sadness may not be a malfunction but a sensitivity to what is genuinely missing. It can be shared with others — and in the sharing it grows lighter.
sadness.practice: Put on a song that carries the sadness of many rather than one — old soul, blues, a choir — and listen to the end. Fisher believed that in such music private sadness becomes shared.

grief.text: The crackle of vinyl beneath a voice long gone from the room — Fisher heard a whole philosophy in that sound. Grief needs no deadlines and no justification. Fisher wrote a great deal about ghosts — not mystical ones but cultural ones: about how the past goes on sounding in the present. He called this “hauntology,” from the word “haunt.” In Ghosts of My Life he describes music that sounds like a memory, like traces of what has gone but won’t let go. Fisher would probably say: the continued presence of what you’ve lost in your life is not a refusal to accept it but a form of faithfulness. Ghosts, as he saw them, don’t just frighten — they preserve what was valuable. Your grief can live beside you as memory, not as a wound that must be closed at once.
grief.practice: Play a recording in which what you lost still lives for you — a song, an old video, someone’s voice — and listen to it in silence, doing nothing else.

loneliness.text: The union club, the shared courtyard, the pub where everyone knew each other — Fisher often recalled places that are growing scarce. Loneliness is painful, and it doesn’t make you weak or strange. He wrote that modern society breaks up older forms of community — trade unions, neighborly ties, shared places — and turns everyone into a separate competitor. At the same time, difficulties are privatized too: everyone thinks they suffer alone. Fisher recalled the practice of “consciousness-raising” — meetings at which people discovered that their “personal” problems were shared. In this light, your loneliness is partly a consequence of how the world is arranged, not evidence that you are unfit for connection. And it can ease simply from discovering that others feel the same.
loneliness.practice: Send a short message to someone you know who may feel the same: “I’m lonely today. How are you?” Fisher saw such admissions as the beginning of community.

anger.text: Where does rage go when it has no address? Fisher’s answer: it returns to sender. Anger is a legitimate response to injustice or powerlessness, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. Fisher noticed something interesting: in today’s world anger often finds no outside target and turns inward. People get angry with themselves for not coping, instead of seeing the circumstances that make “coping” almost impossible. Fisher called one consequence of this “reflexive impotence”: people understand that things are bad but are convinced nothing can be changed — and this conviction becomes self-fulfilling. In this light, your anger is not a destructive force but a sign that you haven’t resigned yourself yet. It can be directed not against yourself but toward understanding what is really wrong.
anger.practice: Walk briskly for five minutes and at every corner silently name one address for your anger — not yourself, but a circumstance: “deadlines,” “money,” “the rules.”

shame.text: A person sits in a seminar room where everyone speaks confidently, and stays silent: it seems they don’t belong there. Fisher’s talk of shame — one of the heaviest feelings — could well begin with this scene. Fisher wrote openly about shame tied to class and background — the feeling of being “out of place,” of having nothing to say in spaces where others feel confident. In his essay “Good For Nothing” he described how society convinces people that their position is entirely deserved, so that their difficulties become a cause for shame. The simple conclusion: part of your shame is society’s internalized judgment, not the truth about you. Seeing this is already a liberation. Shame loses its power when we understand that its source lies not only inside us but in how the hierarchy around us is built.
shame.practice: Write down the sentence your inner voice shames you with, and next to it — where you first heard it: at school, at home, at work. That gives the shame an address.

guilt.text: An economic crisis as personal guilt sounds absurd, yet Fisher showed that this is often how guilt gets handed out: to each person separately. Guilt shows that you care, and that is valuable. But Fisher would help you distinguish guilt over a specific act from a vague, constant feeling that you are “not trying hard enough.” The latter, in his view, is largely created by a culture that loads the individual with responsibility for everything: career, health, well-being, even economic crises. Fisher called this privatization: shared problems are turned into personal failures. Fisher might add: if you’re to blame for everything, something is wrong with the frame itself. Separating real responsibility from imposed guilt can bring relief: the first can be put right, the second can be let go as a burden that isn’t yours.
guilt.practice: Open your palms in front of you: in one, place the specific act that can be put right; in the other, the vague “I’m not trying hard enough.” Lower the second hand to your knee: that weight is not yours.

envy.text: The leaderboard now hangs not only in the office but in every phone — Fisher would explain the abundance of envy today this way. Admitting this unpleasant feeling is already a step toward being honest with yourself. The world he described as “capitalist realism” turns life into an endless competition: for jobs, for attention, for a place in the rankings. When success is considered entirely a personal achievement, every success of someone else’s inevitably sounds like a reproach to you. Here is what follows: envy is not a trait of your character but a natural side effect of a system built on competition. This understanding lets you soften both toward yourself and toward the person you envy: you are both taking part in the same race, which neither of you chose, and perhaps you are both tired of it.
envy.practice: Imagine there are no more rankings — no pay scales, no likes, no grades. Do you still want what this person has? Whatever remains is your desire; the rest is the leaderboard.

emptiness.text: A student at the college where Fisher taught sits in headphones scrolling a feed, though he isn’t enjoying it at all. Emptiness and apathy are exhausting, even when they are hard to explain. Fisher noticed in his students, and in himself, what he called “depressive hedonia”: a person is not so much unable to get pleasure as unable to do anything except pursue it — scroll, switch, consume. And yet there is no deep satisfaction. Fisher linked this to a culture of endless stimulation and to the feeling that the future is closed and there is nothing to strive for. This view can bring relief: your emptiness is not a personal defect but a response to a world in which it is hard to find a large, shared, meaningful cause. And it doesn’t tell the whole truth about you.
emptiness.practice: Spend three minutes on something that isn’t consumption: water a plant, fix a small thing, help a neighbor carry a bag. Fisher set meaningful activity — however tiny — against the endless pursuit of pleasure.

confusion.text: “It’s easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism” — Fisher opens Capitalist Realism with this line. No wonder it’s easy to feel lost in such a world; you needn’t pretend everything is clear. Fisher wrote that one feature of our time is the sense that the existing order of things is the only one possible. He called this “capitalist realism”: an atmosphere in which it is hard even to imagine anything else. Confusion can arise precisely where old explanations stop working and new ones haven’t yet appeared. Confusion here is not a weakness of mind but a moment when the familiar picture of the world cracks. He believed such cracks are valuable — through them you can see that the “natural order” was in fact made by people and could be different. Confusion is the beginning of a new question.
confusion.practice: Pick one thing around you that seems to have “always been this way” — the five-day week, a queue, the news feed — and for a minute imagine how it could be arranged differently. For Fisher, such imagining was where freedom begins.

fatigue.text: A report on how you wrote a report — Fisher met such absurd tasks everywhere and saw them as one cause of mass burnout. Your fatigue is real, and it doesn’t mean you are lazy or weak. He pointed to bureaucracy which, contrary to promises, hasn’t disappeared but has only grown: endless reports, metrics, self-assessments, the need to constantly prove your efficiency. Add to that instability and the feeling that you can’t stop. Fisher insisted that if so many people are exhausted at once, it can’t be explained only by the personal shortcomings of each. This understanding lifts some of the guilt: your fatigue is a response to a real overload. You don’t have to “overcome” it. You can give it room, acknowledge that it’s legitimate, and share it with others who are just as tired.
fatigue.practice: Sit for three minutes doing nothing that could go into a report: no phone, no to-do list, just looking out the window. This time counts for no one — and that is why it is yours.

boredom.text: A hundred channels, a thousand series — and nothing to watch: Fisher saw this paradox as a sign of the times. Boredom can be agonizing, and there’s nothing shameful in it. Fisher described a distinctly modern boredom — not the kind that comes from having nothing to do, but the kind born amid an endless abundance of entertainment. We are constantly plugged into a stream of content, yet nothing truly absorbs us. He wrote about students who couldn’t tear themselves away from their screens but didn’t get any joy from them either. For Fisher, this kind of boredom is not a whim but a sign that the stream of stimuli lacks anything genuinely new. He regretted that culture increasingly repeats the past instead of inventing the future. Your boredom may be a healthy feeling — a longing for something truly new that hasn’t yet been invented.
boredom.practice: Instead of one more clip, find something old that still sounds strange and new — an early electronic recording, an experimental film, a poem — and give it five minutes. Fisher looked for the future in exactly such finds.

quote.text: …the condition I’m referring to is constituted not by an inability to get pleasure so much as by an inability to do anything else except pursue pleasure.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

joy.text: A dance floor where hundreds of people move to one rhythm — for Fisher this was not just a party but an image of another life. Joy is a precious feeling, and you can give yourself to it fully. Fisher, often known as the author of gloomy books, actually thought a great deal about joy. Later he was working on an idea he called “acid communism” — about how to restore to society the capacity for a shared dream and the joy of freeing consciousness. In other words, joy is not just a pleasant sensation but a reminder that life could be different from the familiar routine. It is especially worth cherishing and sharing — shared joy holds the promise of a different future.
joy.practice: Share this joy right now: call someone and tell them about it — or put on music and dance to at least one song, even if your only partner is the room.

love.text: Everything that can’t be bought or sold is already a small act of resistance: this idea runs through all of Fisher’s books, though he never wrote a theory of love. The tenderness you feel is valuable, and you don’t need to be shy about it. He showed how market logic seeps into the most varied spheres of life, turning people into competitors and relationships into deals. Against this background, love and tenderness turn out to be forms of resistance: they don’t submit to calculations of profit, and they bind people together beyond usefulness. Fisher valued solidarity and care as what stands against loneliness and the privatization of suffering. Your tenderness is not a weakness in a harsh world but evidence that human bonds are stronger than the logic of competition. It is worth protecting.
love.practice: Do one thing today for someone close that could never be billed: bring them tea, hear a story out to the end, save them the seat by the window. Fisher would see this as a small step outside the market.

gratitude.text: Pirate radio stations, music magazines, friends’ blogs — that is probably what Fisher would list if asked whom he was grateful to. Gratitude is a warm feeling, and it dismantles the illusion that everyone is self-made. The society he criticized insists that everyone is the sole author of their own fate, and everything achieved is purely personal merit. Gratitude shows the opposite: we live thanks to others — those who taught us, cared for us, made the music and books that sustained us. Fisher himself wrote a lot about how culture and community saved him in hard times. Gratitude brings you back to the understanding that you are part of a web of mutual support, not a lonely entrepreneur of yourself.
gratitude.practice: Find a line from a song or a book that once held you up, and read it aloud — as thanks to those who made it. You could send it to the person who first showed it to you.

hope.text: “The tiniest event can tear a hole in the grey curtain of reaction” — this is how Fisher ends Capitalist Realism. Hope matters most when everything seems frozen. Fisher knew how hard it is to hope: his major book describes an atmosphere in which it is impossible to imagine anything else. Fisher wrote that the very sense that nothing can change makes any change unexpected and powerful. Capitalist realism, in his view, is strong only as long as people believe in it; a small crack is enough for the horizon to open again. In this light, your hope is not naivety but a sober understanding that a world made by people can change. It doesn’t have to be big — it only needs to be enough to keep you from accepting the current state of things as final.
hope.practice: Recall out loud one thing that once seemed impossible and then happened — in your life or in the world. Say it as evidence: the curtain does get holes in it.

quote.text: The tiniest event can tear a hole in the grey curtain of reaction which has marked the horizons of possibility under capitalist realism.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

nostalgia.text: What moved Fisher in an old record was not the past but the future it once promised. Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling, and you don’t need to defend yourself against it. He distinguished two kinds: nostalgia that simply longs for old things, and what he called “hauntology” — a longing not so much for the past as for the futures that past promised but that never arrived. In Ghosts of My Life he hears in the music of his youth the promise of a world that might have been. In this light, your nostalgia may speak not only of what you have lost but also of what you hoped for. This is valuable knowledge: the ghosts of the past keep dreams that can still be brought back into the present.
nostalgia.practice: Play a song from that time and, as you listen, ask yourself not “where did it all go?” but “what did I expect from the future back then?” Fisher called such promises ghosts that can still be summoned.

craving.text: The hand reaches for the screen again with almost no pleasure — Fisher knew the gesture from students and from himself. A sharp “I want it now” can be strong and doesn’t make you weak. Fisher described a state he called “depressive hedonia”: we are not so much unable to get pleasure as unable to do anything except pursue it — one more video, one more cigarette, one more drink, one more refresh of the feed. He saw this not as a personal vice but as a symptom of a culture that offers endless quick stimuli instead of meaning and a shared cause. Fisher might go on: a craving often promises to switch off the background hum of pressure and emptiness for a minute. That doesn’t cancel its force, but it changes the question — not “what’s wrong with me?” but “what am I really missing?” The wave of wanting rises and falls; it can be waited out.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, put a hand on your belly and breathe slowly for three minutes, asking on each out-breath: “If this weren’t a thing but a need — which one: rest, people, meaning?” Meanwhile the wave is changing.

addiction.text: Suffering shared by millions can’t be read as a million “personal problems” — Fisher always insisted on this. If your life has long revolved around something hard to get out of, that is hard, and it is not a moral failure. Fisher criticized “the privatization of stress” — the habit of explaining everything by brain chemistry or willpower while ignoring loneliness, precarious work, a closed-off future. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that addiction often grows where the shared world collapses — community, support, the sense that life could be different. This doesn’t take away the weight of the circle, but it does remove some of the shame. Fisher believed in the power of the collective: that people who recognize shared difficulties together change more easily than they do alone. Getting out of the circle isn’t only a personal feat either; others can take part in it.
addiction.practice: Silently name one person or one place that understands this path from the inside — a mutual-help group, for example. You don’t need to decide anything today: just let a “we” appear in your thoughts alongside the “I.”

hangover.text: Fisher would first check the verdict you pass on yourself the next morning: whose voice is it? A hangover — in body and soul, with anxiety, shame and memory gaps — is hard, and you deserve gentleness. Morning shame usually sounds like a verdict on your whole person: “I’ve ruined everything again.” But Fisher wrote a lot about how society privatizes feelings: everything that happens to us is declared to be solely our fault and our responsibility. It follows that behind last night there is often an understandable wish — to breathe out, to feel part of something shared, to step out for a while from the mode of endless functioning. That wish is legitimate, even if the way it was met has left a heavy mark. Today you don’t need to pass sentence on yourself. You can simply take care of yourself and ask what the real need was.
hangover.practice: Put self-criticism off until tomorrow. Step outside for five minutes and, as you walk, answer one question: what did I really need last night — rest, people, freedom?

euphoria.text: A sudden “anything is possible” in the middle of an ordinary day Fisher saw as a political feeling, not just a personal one. You can simply enjoy this bright flash. He wrote that “capitalist realism” trains us to think there are no alternatives and the future is already closed. Moments of elation when that feeling suddenly lifts he considered precious — especially shared ones: at a concert, in dance, in a conversation where a new idea is born. Fisher would likely note: euphoria is a glimpse of an open future. So that it doesn’t fade without a trace, it helps not only to live it but to remember it: what exactly seemed possible? Whom would you like to share it with? A question like that turns a flash into something you can come back to later.
euphoria.practice: Say one sentence out loud: “In this moment it seemed possible to me that…” — and finish it. If someone is nearby, say it to them; if not, remember it to repeat on an ordinary day.

crash.text: Fisher would describe a grey Monday after a bright Sunday as a small copy of what happened to a whole culture. When the world turns grey again after a high, it is very painful, and it is not your fault. Following Franco “Bifo” Berardi, he spoke of “the slow cancellation of the future”: the feeling that the bright tomorrow we were promised never arrived and life has fallen back into the usual rut. For you this means: the comedown is hard partly because the high was a glimpse of another possibility, and the drop seems to prove there isn’t one. But Fisher insisted: greyness is not the nature of things but a condition that changes. What you saw during the high was not an illusion but a hint. For now, you can simply wait it out and take care of yourself.
crash.practice: Do one small thing with someone today — take a walk, have tea, help each other with some little task. Fisher believed greyness is easier to bear when you are not alone.

panic.text: Millions of people know these minutes: your heart pounds, you can’t get enough air, it seems something irreversible is about to happen. It is very hard, and you are not alone in it. Fisher would point out that millions of people go through such states today, and he saw in this not only a personal but a social dimension: constant uncertainty, instability, living “braced for the next blow.” He said that stress has been privatized — everyone carries it alone, as if it were their own private malfunction. Right now, in the middle of the wave, explanations aren’t the main thing. The main thing is that a wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don’t have to fight it; you can wait it out, leaning on your body, on the floor beneath your feet, on what is around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and make each out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name five objects around you out loud, and then, if you can, rest your palm on something warm or call someone whose voice calms you.

dread.text: An empty Suffolk shore, an abandoned station, a wood that’s too quiet — Fisher called such places eerie. The question “what is it all for,” the sense of an abyss, is among the deepest human experiences, and it doesn’t make you weak. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher wrote about feelings that arise at the edge of the familiar world: the “weird” — the presence of something that doesn’t belong here — and the “eerie” — the sense that something unfathomable lies behind what we see. These experiences are unsettling, but Fisher also saw value in them: they let us look at the familiar from outside and understand that the world is bigger than our routines. Seen through Fisher’s eyes, your dread is also an encounter with a vastness that everyday life usually screens off. In it you can not only get lost but also find questions that give life back its depth.
dread.practice: Go out for five minutes to somewhere empty and quiet — a yard, a vacant lot, a riverbank — and simply listen. Fisher believed an encounter with the eerie doesn’t only frighten but also enlarges the world.

fomo.text: Someone is at a concert right now, someone in the mountains, someone celebrating — and you feel you are in the wrong place. Fisher would ask: who arranged things so that you see all this around the clock? Fisher wrote a lot about digital culture, in which we are always “connected” and always see other people’s lives in their best shots. He noted that such an environment turns everyone into an entrepreneur of their own life, forced to constantly compare and sell themselves. Translated into the language of your life, the fear of missing out is neither personal envy nor foolishness, but a response to the design of an environment that deliberately keeps a sense of lack alive. A great many people share this feeling with you — including those whose pictures make you envious. Realizing this is already a relief: you are not the only one “in the wrong place.”
fomo.practice: Move one app off your home screen until tomorrow, and spend the freed-up five minutes where you are: look out the window, talk to whoever is nearby.

sleepless.text: A work email at midnight, a notification at two — Fisher wrote about “flexible” work that doesn’t end when the working day does. A sleepless night of circling thoughts is exhausting, and it is not your fault. Jonathan Crary developed a related idea in his book 24/7, where sleep is described as the last thing that resists the demand to be always available. Fisher might put it this way: night-time anxiety is also an echo of life without clear boundaries, not only your personal inability to “switch off.” At three in the morning everything looks darker than it is. The thoughts that come at that hour don’t have to be solved now.
sleepless.practice: Put your phone out of reach and tell yourself: “This is a question for daylight.” Then breathe in for a count of four and out for six, until you notice your body growing heavier.

betrayal.text: Solidarity, trust, the ability to lean on one another — Fisher thought about them constantly, though he didn’t write about personal betrayal as such. So he would understand this pain: what collapses is not only your bond with a person but the feeling that you can lean on others. He showed how contemporary culture trains us to see others as competitors and to treat relationships as deals. In such an environment trust becomes especially fragile — and especially precious. Yet Fisher never gave up his belief in solidarity: he thought people are capable of genuine mutuality if the conditions for it are created. One person’s betrayal doesn’t cancel that possibility. Your capacity to trust is not naivety but what everything good between people rests on.
betrayal.practice: Think of one person who once didn’t let you down, and call them or simply thank them in your mind. One betrayal doesn’t cancel the whole web of trust.

jealousy.text: A dating app always has one more profile, and Fisher would likely see in this a market where everything is compared, rated and replaceable. Jealousy, agonizing and very human, gets extra fuel in such a world. Even love starts, without our meaning it to, to look like competition — with others, with imagined “better options.” Hence the fear that you might be “traded in.” This doesn’t mean your jealousy is imagined: there is a great deal of real attachment and vulnerability in it. But it helps to notice which part of the fear belongs not only to you but to a general background of comparison and insecurity. Relationships, as Fisher saw it, can be a place where this market logic doesn’t apply.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself out loud: “What am I really afraid of — losing this person, or turning out to be ‘not good enough’?” If it’s the second, say: “I am not an item on a shelf.”

resentment.text: In the 1970s, women gathered in kitchens and found that their “personal” grievances were strikingly alike; Fisher considered this practice, consciousness-raising, one of the most important. An old grievance is a weight you carry, and it often keeps the memory of a real injustice. Taking Fisher’s thought further, a grievance becomes especially heavy when we carry it alone and see in it only a personal story between two people. When you manage to see the wider context too — the power, inequality and pressure that everyone involved was under — the grievance doesn’t vanish, but it can stop eating away at you from the inside. Your sense of justice is valuable; it can be directed not only at the past but at what can still be changed.
resentment.practice: Tell this story to someone you trust, but begin not with the person but with the circumstances: “It all happened at a time when…”. Notice how the weight changes.

heartbreak.text: The muffled voices on Burial’s records sound like echoes of nights gone by and people lost — Fisher heard them as the music of ghosts. A broken heart really hurts, and there’s no need to hurry that pain along. Fisher wrote a great deal about “hauntology” — about how we are haunted by ghosts: a past that won’t let go, and unrealized futures that keep sounding. Fisher would probably say: after a breakup the person becomes such a ghost for us, and with them the future you had imagined together. Grieving it is natural. Fisher showed that ghosts don’t only wound: they preserve what was valuable. In time they can become not pain but memory.
heartbreak.practice: Walk for five minutes along an evening street and let memories surface and fade like muffled voices on an old recording. Don’t hold on to them and don’t chase them away.

impostor.text: A diploma on the wall, experience behind you — and still the feeling that you’re about to be found out: Fisher knew well where this voice comes from. In his essay “Good For Nothing,” he wrote about how class background and social position shape the feeling that you have no right to be where you are — at university, in a profession, in a conversation. This feeling is instilled over years, and then it sounds like your own voice. The simple conclusion: impostor syndrome is often not the truth about you but the trace of social hierarchies that decide in advance who “belongs” and who is an “outsider.” Once you recognize this mechanism, you can step back from your fear a little: it’s loud, but it isn’t a judge.
impostor.practice: Say out loud, as if at a meeting, three specific things you did to get where you are now. No “I was lucky,” no “just.”

self_hatred.text: The voice that whispers “you’re worthless” sounds like your own — Fisher suggested checking where it got its accent. If your inner voice is cruel to you, that is very hard, and you deserve compassion — including from yourself. Fisher wrote openly about dark states and about the voice that insists you are good for nothing. He came to the view that this voice is largely absorbed from outside: society teaches us to blame ourselves for things tied to inequality, instability and constant evaluation. In his essay “Good For Nothing,” he showed how a sense of one’s own worthlessness can be a reflection of social position rather than a person’s essence. Fisher might add: your inner critic speaks in a voice you didn’t invent. You don’t have to believe it.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic, and next to it — whose voice it speaks in: a teacher’s, a boss’s, an advert’s. Read both lines aloud.

helplessness.text: “We know things are bad, but we can’t do anything about it” — Fisher met this thought in his students so often that he gave it a name. Helplessness is a heavy feeling, and it deserves compassion. Fisher described a similar state in his students and called it “reflexive impotence.” People understand that much is badly arranged, and “know” just as clearly that they can do nothing about it. But Fisher noticed something important: this knowledge is not a neutral observation but partly a self-fulfilling prophecy. The certainty of being powerless itself keeps us from acting. Here is what follows: your powerlessness is real, but it isn’t the whole truth. Much really is beyond your control — and that isn’t your fault. But sometimes a single small action is enough for the prophecy to stop coming true.
helplessness.practice: Do one tiny thing right now that is surely within your power: tidy one corner, call one person, take out the trash. Fisher would say: this is how the prophecy of powerlessness stops coming true.

quote.text: They know things are bad, but more than that, they know they can’t do anything about it. But that “knowledge”, that reflexivity, is not a passive observation of an already existing state of affairs. It is a self-fulfilling prophecy.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

procrastination.text: A form in which you must describe how you plan to fill in another form — Fisher found such tasks everywhere and wasn’t surprised that nobody wants to start them. “I can’t get started” is not laziness or a character flaw. Fisher wrote about how work and study are saturated with endless reports, metrics and audits — he called this “market Stalinism”: the system cares more about how a result looks than about the work itself. When a task seems like a pointless formality, starting it is especially hard. Fisher also described “depressive hedonia” — the constant pull of quick stimuli that makes concentration agonizing. In other words, your procrastination may signal not weakness but a loss of meaning, or overload. You can ask yourself not “why am I like this?” but “what about this task drains its meaning for me?”
procrastination.practice: Ask out loud: “Why does this task matter to me — not for the report, but for me?” If you find an answer, work for two minutes; if not, that too is honest knowledge.

uprooted.text: The smell of a street, the neighbors’ accent, the clang of a tram — Fisher would call them ghosts that keep sounding in a person after a move. Being cut off from home changes life profoundly, and your sense of loss is legitimate. In Ghosts of My Life Fisher described how we are haunted by ghosts — of a past that won’t let go, and of futures that never arrived. Fisher also showed how the modern world demands “flexibility” and mobility, forcing people to keep moving and adapting. Fisher might go on: your uprootedness is not only a personal failure to adapt but a shared experience of the age. The ghosts of home are not enemies; they keep what was dear to you.
uprooted.practice: Find the sound of that place, in memory or in a recording — a tram, a market, speech in your native language — and listen to it for a minute with your eyes closed. The ghosts of home are not enemies.

overload.text: How many signals have you taken in since morning — hundreds, thousands? Fisher considered this a political question, not only a personal one. Overload from such a stream is real exhaustion, not an inability to “cope.” Fisher, following Franco “Bifo” Berardi, wrote about the overloading of the “infosphere”: the volume of signals demanding attention has long exceeded what a person can process. He noticed in his students a state of constant connection — phone, headphones, feed — with not a minute of silence or concentration. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that your exhaustion is the nervous system’s natural response to an environment deliberately designed to hold attention. This is not a personal weakness. The way out isn’t learning to consume even more, even faster, but stepping out of the stream from time to time — and knowing you’re not alone in this.
overload.practice: Mute everything for five minutes, close your eyes and listen only to what sounds without a screen: the street, your breathing, the house.

unreality.text: A reality that seems like the only possible one is the main character of all Fisher’s books. So he would understand how strange and unsettling it can be to feel that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real. His “capitalist realism” is the idea that the familiar order of things seems to us the only possible and natural one, even though it was largely made by people and could be different. In The Weird and the Eerie, he described experiences in which the familiar world suddenly looks alien. It follows that a sense of unreality sometimes arises when the familiar picture of the world loses its persuasiveness. It’s frightening, but it doesn’t make you “abnormal.” You can gently lean on what is tangible here and now: your body, sounds, objects, people.
unreality.practice: Name out loud three sounds you can hear and three things you can touch, and rest your palm on the warmest of them.

awe.text: Reports, tasks, deadlines — and suddenly a sky without edges: Fisher valued the moments when such vastness breaks through the everyday. This rare experience is worth living to the full. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher wrote about the feelings that arise when we meet what lies beyond the familiar. He noted that such experiences don’t only unsettle but also fascinate: they let us see the familiar world from outside and feel that it is bigger than our routines. Fisher would likely note: awe is the moment when the “realism” of everyday life, with its reports and tasks, suddenly stops being the only reality. Something vast opens up — the sea, the sky, music, another person’s thought. Fisher valued such moments as a reminder that the world is neither exhausted nor closed.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what moved you, then say out loud one word for how the world seemed to you in that moment. Let that word be evidence that the world is not closed.

relief.text: A room in which someone says, “Me too” — Fisher considered such moments among the most freeing. Something heavy has finally let go, and this is a warm, well-earned feeling. Fisher wrote a lot about the relief that comes when a person realizes their difficulties are shared by others. He called this “consciousness-raising”: when people tell each other about their experiences, private, shameful pain turns into something shared, understandable and explicable. For you this means: relief is the moment when the burden stops being yours alone. Even if you experience it in solitude, there is something of that discovery in it: life is bigger than you thought at the hardest moment. You can remember this moment — and share it with someone.
relief.practice: If you like, tell someone in one sentence that you feel lighter — out loud or in a message. Relief shared with another sounds louder.

calm.text: A minute without notifications seems almost a luxury today; Fisher didn’t write about calm specifically, but he knew the value of silence well. The calm you feel now is precious, and you can simply be in it. Fisher criticized an environment with not a minute of silence, and dreamed of a life in which people have time not only to work and consume but simply to be, to think, to listen. Your calm is a small piece of such a life. It doesn’t need to be used for anything or justified. You can simply notice it and let it last — as a reminder that another rhythm of life is possible already, right now.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute without touching your phone and listen to how the place you’re in sounds: near sounds, far ones, the quietest. This is the other rhythm of life Fisher dreamed of.

inspiration.text: A sound no one has heard yet — Fisher waited for it from music and culture and rejoiced at every such glimpse. Inspiration is a lively, joyful feeling, and it’s worth meeting with gratitude. Fisher wrote about “the slow cancellation of the future” — the sense that instead of new forms we endlessly recycle old ones. He saw the opposite of this in “popular modernism”: times when bold, experimental ideas reached huge numbers of people through music, books and television. Seen through Fisher’s eyes, your inspiration is a small breakthrough of the future into the present, a glimpse of what hasn’t existed yet. It’s worth protecting, without rushing to fit it to familiar measures of success. Sometimes the most valuable thing about a new idea is that it doesn’t yet resemble anything.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea and one sentence about what is genuinely new in it — what you haven’t seen before. Don’t decide yet what it will be good for.

schadenfreude.text: The shameful pleasure at someone else’s failure Fisher would treat not as a character flaw but as a symptom. Fisher wrote about “business ontology” — the conviction that everything in society, from hospitals to schools, should be run like a business. In such an environment life turns into an endless competition: at work, in education, even on social media, everyone is rated against everyone else. Someone else’s failure then easily feels like a small breather: “at least I’m not last.” Translated into the language of your life, schadenfreude is not only your personal trait but an effect of an environment that sets people against one another. That is no reason to punish yourself, but a reason to notice: you and the one who stumbled are most likely under the same pressure.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine for a minute that you and the person who stumbled are standing in the same queue at the same window. What is pressing on you both?

contempt.text: Who really wins when people with similar troubles despise one another? Fisher asked this again and again. Contempt gives a sense of being in the right and of distance, and sometimes it is a defense when something cuts deep. In his well-known essay “Exiting the Vampire Castle,” Fisher criticized an atmosphere in which people take pleasure in publicly condemning and despising others, displaying their own purity. He believed such contempt divides people who in fact share many of the same difficulties, and changes almost nothing for the better. Fisher might put it this way: contempt is often aimed at people who are closer to us than they seem. There’s no need to shame yourself for it. But it helps to ask why you and the person you despise ended up on opposite sides. Sometimes a shared weariness shows through the contempt.
contempt.practice: Think of one difficulty that you and the person you despise most likely share, and say it out loud. Just one is enough.

disgust.text: The self-checkout machine politely announcing an “unexpected item in the bagging area” — Fisher saw the face of an era in such trifles. Disgust is a strong, bodily feeling, and it can be very honest. Fisher spoke ironically of “boring dystopia” — an everyday life in which everything more or less works but provokes a dull revulsion: endless advertising, pointless forms and reports, empty corporate slogans. Taking Fisher’s thought further, disgust is sometimes a healthy reaction to what is genuinely unacceptable, a way of refusing to accept “that’s just how things are.” And if it is turned against yourself, Fisher would remind you: society readily teaches people to despise their own “failures,” even though their causes often lie beyond the person. Your disgust is worth listening to: what does it really concern — you, or the circumstances you have to live in?
disgust.practice: Notice one “boring dystopia” scene today — an ad, a form, a corporate slogan — and say to yourself out loud: “This turns my stomach, and that’s an honest reaction.”

revenge.text: Revenge stories draw millions of viewers while the conditions that make people cruel stay off screen — Fisher would notice that. The wish for revenge is an understandable response to pain and injustice. Fisher noticed that our culture tends to reduce every conflict to personal scores: a particular person is to blame, and payback must be personal. Fisher would probably say: the thirst for revenge is often aimed at whoever happened to be closest, even though the source of the pain is wider — in conditions that make people hard, worn out and indifferent to one another. This doesn’t excuse the person who hurt you or devalue your feeling. But Fisher invited us to look beyond individuals: personal revenge almost never changes what gives rise to such situations. The energy of this feeling can turn into clarity — about what was unjust and what you need in order to feel safe.
revenge.practice: Clench your fists for a count of five, unclench them on the out-breath, and repeat three times. Then name out loud what you need to feel safe — without involving the person who hurt you.

anger_at_loved.text: The front door doesn’t stop the pressure of work, debt and competition — Fisher would show how it comes in with you. Hence the anger at those close to you, and the shame that follows. Fisher spoke of “the privatization of stress”: society declares the pressure of precarious work, debt and constant competition to be everyone’s private business. And that pressure comes home. Home becomes the place where tension built up outside spills over — simply because there’s nowhere else for it to go. The simple conclusion: your anger at loved ones is not proof that you love badly, but often the trace of a load you have to carry alone. Understanding this doesn’t excuse harsh words, but it lifts some of the guilt and helps you see: you need support, and the people close to you are not enemies but equally tired people beside you.
anger_at_loved.practice: Before you go in at home, stand by the door for a minute and mentally leave outside what you brought with you: the boss, the bills, the crowd. Take three out-breaths — and only then open it.

ambivalence.text: How many roles do you expect one person to play — friend, doctor, therapist, family? Fisher would ask this before talking about feelings. Loving someone and not being able to stand them is hard, but nothing is wrong with you. Fisher wrote about how the disappearance of collective forms of support shifts the whole weight of life onto individuals. Fisher might add: today the closest relationships often have to stand in for everything at once — support, rest, help and meaning. Under such a load any bond starts to crack. Your ambivalence partly reflects the fact that too much is expected of one person, and that you depend on each other more than you would like. In such a situation love and irritation inevitably intertwine. You can acknowledge both feelings, and consider what load this relationship is carrying for everything that’s missing around it.
ambivalence.practice: In your mind, hand out this person’s roles to other people in your life: who could take on even one — listening, helping, cheering you up? Imagine how much lighter it would be for you both.

guilty_relief.text: A carer no one ever relieves — Fisher would show that many people live this way, even if they never use the word. Relief when the load lifts — after a breakup, a job, or long care for a sick loved one — often comes with sharp guilt. Fisher reminded us how much society shifts onto the shoulders of individuals: caring for the sick, supporting the family, surviving at an exhausting job are all considered private matters that each person must shoulder alone. Under such a load a person becomes depleted, even when they love deeply. Here is what follows: your relief is not evidence of callousness but a natural response to having a burden lifted that was too much for one person. The guilt here is often an echo of the idea that you were obliged to cope endlessly and without help. Love and relief can live side by side. One doesn’t cancel the other.
guilty_relief.practice: List out loud everything you carried alone during that time — and listen to the list as if a close friend were telling it.

indifference.text: News of a disaster between an ad and a meme — Fisher wrote about an environment where everything comes in one stream and so nothing touches us. When something that “should” move you leaves only emptiness inside, that is frightening. Fisher described a state many people live in: the stream of news, notifications and entertainment never stops, and feelings seem to grow dull. He wrote about his students, who, as he observed, lived in a mode of constant overload and distraction and could barely concentrate on anything. In other words, your indifference is not necessarily a trait of character but a consequence of an environment that demands you react to everything at once. No psyche can respond endlessly. There’s no need to force yourself to feel “the right way.” You can reduce the stream and give feeling time to return once there’s space.
indifference.practice: Pick one thing from the stream — a news item, a photo, a song — and give it five minutes without switching. If no feeling comes, that’s all right: you have made room for it.

escape.text: “There is no alternative” — Fisher saw this phrase as the motto of an era. So the wish to drop everything — job, city, role — and leave often comes to those tired of that “no.” In that light, the dream of escape is not weakness but resistance to the feeling that nothing could be otherwise, a way of saying: “there has to be something else.” Fisher valued such utopian impulses and believed that the ability to imagine something different is the first step toward change. Fisher might go on: there’s no need to break everything immediately. But the wish to escape deserves to be heard seriously: it points to something in the current shape of your life that really is unbearable. You can begin with a question: what exactly do I want to leave behind, and what do I want to find?
escape.practice: Take a five-minute escape: walk a different way from home than usual and notice what looks unfamiliar. Fisher believed the ability to see otherwise starts with small things.

forbidden_attraction.text: A door behind which a whole other world begins — a favorite image in the weird tales Fisher studied. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and disorienting. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher describes the “weird” as that which doesn’t fit the familiar order — an intrusion of something from outside, after which familiar frames suddenly stop seeming the only ones possible. He stressed that such an experience doesn’t only unsettle but also fascinates. Apply this to yourself, and it turns out that attraction to the “wrong” person is often exactly such an encounter with the weird — with something beyond your ordinary life. There’s no need either to condemn it or to rush to do anything about it. You can simply ask yourself: what other possibility, what “outside world,” does this person embody for me?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Picture this attraction as a door rather than a person: what world, what life or what part of yourself do you see behind it? Sometimes you can enter that world by another way.

social_anxiety.text: Who in this room decided you don’t belong? That is how Fisher would ask. Fearing people’s judgment is agonizing, and any gathering can become an ordeal. Fisher wrote candidly about the feeling of being out of place: in his essay “Good For Nothing” he described how someone from a family without much money feels like an outsider in spaces where others carry themselves with confidence. He showed that such insecurity is not only a personal trait but the trace of a social hierarchy that from childhood hints at who is “fitting” and who is not. It follows that part of your fear of judgment is the internalized voice of that hierarchy. Recognizing it is already a relief. And one more thing: a great many people in the room feel the same, it’s just not the done thing to show it. Your shyness doesn’t mean you don’t belong here.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a gathering, press your feet into the floor and tell yourself: “Many people here feel the same; they just don’t show it.” At the gathering, look for one person who is also standing on the edge.

uncertainty.text: Can a life be built out of short stretches — a six-month contract, a one-year lease? Fisher doubted it. Uncertainty is exhausting: it’s hard to make plans when you don’t know what will happen. In Capitalist Realism, Fisher cites the sociologist Richard Sennett and his formula “no long term”: modern work and life are increasingly organized around short-term contracts, constant change and the absence of guarantees. Fisher believed this produces chronic anxiety in enormous numbers of people. In this light, your uncertainty is not only a personal inability to “plan everything out” but a shared condition of the times. This matters: you are not alone in it and not to blame. Fisher also reminded us that the future is not closed for good: uncertainty also means things may turn out differently from the worst forecasts.
uncertainty.practice: Name out loud one thing that depends on you today and one that doesn’t. Do the first; let the second go for today.

waiting.text: “Your call is important to us” — Fisher heard a whole philosophy of bureaucracy in that phrase. Waiting for an answer, results or news is sometimes harder than even the worst certainty. In Capitalist Realism, Fisher described a Kafkaesque experience everyone knows: calling a call center, endless hold music, being passed from one operator to another — and no one able to decide anything. He saw in this an image of modern bureaucracy, where responsibility is diffuse and all a person can do is wait. Fisher would likely note: part of what makes waiting so agonizing is a feeling of powerlessness before an impersonal system, not your impatience. It’s not your fault. You can acknowledge, “Right now nothing depends on me,” — and reclaim at least what does: how you spend this hour.
waiting.practice: While you wait, choose one thing for the next five minutes that belongs only to you: take a walk, stretch, listen to one song. Waiting won’t take this whole hour from you.

regret.text: The version of a life that could have happened but didn’t follows a person around like a ghost — Fisher found a special word for such ghosts. Regret over what you didn’t do often feels exactly like such an encounter. Fisher used the word “hauntology” (from the French hanter, “to haunt”) for the experience of being unable to shake off futures that never came to pass. He wrote about it in relation to culture, but the idea applies to personal life too. Importantly, Fisher didn’t see such ghosts only as a burden: they remind us that something else was possible, and so is possible now. In this light, your regret is not simply self-reproach but the trace of a desire that is still alive. You can ask: what did I really want back then — and is there a path for that desire today?
regret.practice: Write down what you really wanted back then, and next to it — one small action open to that desire today.

longing.text: A distant melody that plays even when all around is quiet — Fisher knew how to hear such melodies in other people’s songs. Missing a particular person sounds much like this inside. Fisher wrote a lot about music in which loss can be heard — for example, Burial’s album Untrue, where fragments of voices sound like ghosts of the past. For him such music conveys a particular feeling: the presence of someone who isn’t there. For you this means: your longing is not a malfunction to be fixed as soon as possible, but a form of connection with someone who is absent. Fisher valued culture’s capacity to give such feelings a voice rather than drown them out. It may help to find your own “music” of longing — a song, a place, words — where this feeling can sound instead of staying mute inside you.
longing.practice: Find one song that sounds like your longing for this person, and listen to it in the half-dark, doing nothing else — the way Fisher listened to records full of ghosts.

world_pain.text: What do you do with pain that can’t be carried alone? Fisher’s answer: don’t carry it alone. Wars, injustice and grim news can wound deeply and wear you out. Fisher warned about “reflexive impotence”: knowing that everything is bad, combined with the conviction that nothing can be done. Such a conviction, in his view, confirms itself. At the same time, he didn’t suggest taking everything on yourself: Fisher stressed the importance of the collective — thinking things through together, mutual support, shared causes. In this light, your pain is a sign that you haven’t grown callous, and that is valuable. Relief comes when the pain is shared with others and finds at least a small, manageable expression: a conversation, some help, taking part in something shared.
world_pain.practice: Talk today with one person you trust about what troubles you in the world. Don’t look for solutions — just share it.

rejection.text: An unanswered CV, a swipe left, “unfortunately we have chosen another candidate” — Fisher saw in this not a string of private failures but the regime of a whole era. When you are rejected, it seems you have been told the final truth about yourself. People are constantly being evaluated, and every refusal is easily read as personal inadequacy. Fisher criticized this habit of explaining everything by individual shortcomings while ignoring how the environment is built. Seen through Fisher’s eyes, rejection often speaks of how selection works — the number of applicants, chance, other people’s criteria — rather than of your worth. The pain of it is real and deserves attention. But you can put off drawing conclusions about yourself: you are not reducible to a committee’s decision or someone else’s “no.”
rejection.practice: List out loud three circumstances that may have shaped this “no” and have nothing to do with your worth: the number of applicants, someone else’s criteria, chance.

abandonment.text: How many people could you lean on if one disappeared? Fisher would ask without reproach. The fear of being abandoned can be very strong and very old. Fisher wrote about how modern life leaves people less and less protected: temporary work, frequent moves, the weakening of shared institutions of support. When there is little that’s stable around you, you hold tighter to the few close bonds you have — and fear losing them, because there’s nothing else to lean on. Translated into the language of your life, your fear is not only personal vulnerability but a response to a general shortage of reliability. This lifts some of the shame about it. And it also suggests a way forward: support can rest not on one person but on a network — friends, a community, shared causes. Fisher believed in the power of the collective, where no one has to hold on alone.
abandonment.practice: Send a short message to a person or a community you’ve long wanted to be closer to: just “How are you?” or “Can I join you?”. Support is a web, not a single thread.

unrequited.text: Half the songs in any chart are about love that went unanswered, and Fisher saw this not as chance but as consolation. Your feeling goes on living without an answer, and it hurts. Fisher wrote a lot about pop music and how it gives voice to exactly such experiences: songs of love without return are one of its richest traditions. For him culture is a space where private pain turns out to be shared: listening to a song, you realize someone has already felt exactly this. Fisher might put it this way: unrequited love is not a personal failure but one of the most common human experiences. Your feeling is real, even if it wasn’t returned. Let yourself lean on those who have expressed something similar — in a song, a book, a film — and feel that you are not alone in this.
unrequited.practice: Find a poem or a song lyric about unrequited love that hits your feeling exactly, and read it aloud. Someone has already felt precisely this.

humiliation.text: You can strip a person of dignity without shouting — with a questionnaire, an audit, endless evaluation: Fisher knew this well. Such a feeling can stay in the body for a long time. Fisher wrote about how modern institutions often humiliate people in routine ways: endless audits, reports, evaluations, interviews in which a person must prove again and again their right to a place. He called this bureaucracy of metrics “market Stalinism” — a system in which the numbers matter more than the real work. In such an environment many people feel humiliated even though no one in particular set out to humiliate them. Taking Fisher’s thought further, humiliation is often built into the system rather than caused by your inadequacy. And if a particular person humiliated you, that speaks of how they use power, not of your worth.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself about the situation out loud, starting not with yourself but with the circumstances: “I was put in a position where…”. Listen to how your voice changes.

body_shame.text: An ad that first finds a flaw in you and then sells you the cure — Fisher saw in this the mechanism of a whole era. Being unhappy with your body rarely comes out of nowhere. Fisher wrote about how the logic of the market seeps into the most personal areas of life: a person begins to treat themselves as a project that must constantly be improved, promoted and compared with others. Fisher would probably say: in such a culture the body too becomes “capital” — something to invest in, judged through other people’s eyes. And constant dissatisfaction with yourself is convenient for the market: it keeps you looking for ever new ways to “fix” yourself. Understanding this doesn’t cancel your feelings, but it removes some of the guilt from them. Your body is not a business project but what you live, feel and connect with others through.
body_shame.practice: Notice one ad or image today that made you feel worse in your body, and say out loud: “This is a sale, not the truth.” Then rest a palm on your shoulder and thank your body for one step it took today.

illness.text: “Out of action” is a military phrase, and Fisher would notice how easily we apply it to illness. When your body lets you down, fear, irritation and fatigue arrive — and often guilt. Fisher wrote about a culture that demands a person always be in shape, connected and productive. In it, illness is experienced not only as suffering but as personal failure. Speaking of mental health difficulties, Fisher insisted that the blame for them cannot be placed entirely on the individual; this idea can be extended to physical illness as well. The simple conclusion: being ill doesn’t mean letting others down. You don’t have to apologize for your body needing time and care. And the help you accept now is not a debt but part of the shared fabric in which people support one another.
illness.practice: If someone offers you help, answer simply “thank you” — no apologies, no explanations. The care you accept is part of a shared fabric.

pride.text: “It worked” is a short phrase, but Fisher would hear in it an argument with years of inner verdicts. Pride in what you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling. Fisher wrote a great deal about how people, especially from less well-off backgrounds, are taught to think they are “good for nothing,” and how this idea, absorbed in childhood, saps their strength. Against this background, healthy pride in what you’ve done is not vanity but a small act of resistance to an inner verdict. Fisher might add: pride also matters because it pushes back against “reflexive impotence” — the conviction that nothing will work out. You did it — so something did work out. Fisher also valued collective joy, so this kind of pride can be shared: tell people who will be glad with you about what you’ve done.
pride.practice: Tell one person today about what you managed to do — no “but,” no downplaying. For Fisher, joy shared like this is a small piece of the collective.

melancholy.text: The hiss of an old cassette, an empty station at night, a song that sounds like a memory of the future — Fisher built Ghosts of My Life out of such images. Gentle sadness is a feeling that holds both sorrow and tenderness. Following the Italian philosopher Franco “Bifo” Berardi, Fisher spoke of “the slow cancellation of the future” — the sense that the new things once promised never arrived. But Fisher distinguished between a melancholy that resigns itself and one that refuses to forget what was possible. The second keeps the memory that life could have been different — and so still can be. In this light, your gentle sadness is a form of faithfulness to what matters. There’s no need to drive it away: a hope lives in it that hasn’t yet found its words.
melancholy.practice: Write down which “never-happened” you are grieving, and next to it — what in it still seems valuable and possible to you.

quote.text: The slow cancellation of the future
quote.author: Franco “Bifo” Berardi
quote.source: a phrase Fisher develops in Ghosts of My Life
